name: Singapore
note: Since 2022 the family does not register a death: the hospital, relatives or occupier must report it to a doctor, and the doctor must submit the cause and particulars to the Registrar-General (ICA) within 24 hours, electronically. Reportable deaths go to the police and Coroner, whose certificate drives registration. ICA issues the death certificate and controls extracts, which licensed insurers may obtain directly. ICA also keeps the NRIC register, and CPF savings pass to nominees or the Public Trustee, but the notification links to CPF and other agencies could not be confirmed from official pages here.

steps.title: Responsible person reports the death to a doctor
steps.who: The hospital (deaths in hospital); otherwise relatives present and occupiers of the premises; the master of a conveyance; or relatives, persons present and anyone taking charge of the body.
steps.trigger: A death that is not, or does not appear to be, a reportable death.

deadline.text: as soon as practicable after the death

steps.summary: Every non-reportable death in Singapore must be reported to a medical practitioner; failing to do so is an offence (fine up to S$1,500 or one month's imprisonment). One responsible person's report discharges the others.

steps.title: Doctor examines the body and establishes the history
steps.who: The medical practitioner who received the report.
steps.trigger: Report of a death under s. 22(3).
steps.summary: The doctor must examine the body and ascertain the medical history and circumstances to decide whether the death is reportable.

steps.title: Reportable deaths reported to the police
steps.who: Any person (including a doctor) who becomes aware of a reportable death (as defined in the Coroners Act Second Schedule).
steps.trigger: A death that is or appears to be reportable (e.g. unnatural, sudden or unexplained).
steps.summary: Reportable deaths go to the police, not the ordinary route; failure to report is an offence.

steps.title: Police investigate; Coroner's certificate issued
steps.who: Police officers, then a Coroner (with forensic pathologists).
steps.summary: The police must go to the scene and investigate; the Coroner (or a forensic pathologist's findings) then supplies the basis for registration.

steps.title: Doctor submits cause of death and particulars to the Registrar-General
steps.who: The examining medical practitioner, to the Registrar-General of Births and Deaths (ICA).

deadline.text: within 24 hours after examining the body

steps.summary: For non-reportable deaths registration is driven by the doctor, not the family: the doctor must give the cause of death and death particulars to the Registrar-General within 24 hours (offence: fine up to S$1,000), using the electronic service the Registrar-General specifies.

steps.title: Coroner's certificate or pathologist's particulars go to the Registrar-General
steps.who: The Coroner, or the pathologist/forensic pathologist who examined the body.
steps.trigger: Issue of a Coroner's certificate or pathologist's findings.
steps.summary: For reportable deaths the Registrar-General registers on the pathologist's particulars or the Coroner's certificate, and may register before a certificate where the body cannot be recovered or no certificate is needed.

steps.title: Registrar-General registers the death
steps.who: The Registrar-General of Births and Deaths (ICA).
steps.trigger: Receipt of the doctor's particulars, pathologist's particulars or Coroner's certificate.
steps.summary: The Registrar-General must register the death as soon as practicable and keeps the register of deaths, which is not open to public inspection.

steps.title: Death certificate issued
steps.who: The Registrar-General, to such person as it thinks fit (in practice the next of kin, as a digital certificate).
steps.summary: After registration the Registrar-General may issue a death certificate in the form and to the person it thinks fit.

steps.title: Extracts of the death record for eligible persons
steps.who: Parents, spouse, children, siblings, grandparents, grandchildren, administrators/executors; others only with a legitimate interest.
steps.summary: Extracts from the register go to listed relatives and personal representatives; anyone else must show an interest of the estate or another legitimate interest.

steps.title: Licensed insurers may obtain an extract of the death record
steps.who: A licensed insurer that is party to an insurance contract relating to the deceased.
steps.trigger: An insurance claim or contract relating to the deceased.
steps.summary: Licensed insurers are 'eligible persons' who may apply directly to the Registrar-General for an extract, an official route for insurers to verify a death without the family. No equivalent route for banks was found.

steps.title: Burial or cremation only at licensed cemeteries and crematoria
steps.who: Undertakers/families, at NEA-provided or licensed cemeteries and crematoria.
steps.summary: Burial and cremation are lawful only in places provided by the National Environment Agency or licensed under the Act. Whether a registered death certificate is the permit for burial or cremation could not be confirmed from statute text.

steps.title: Death recorded against the NRIC in the national register
steps.who: ICA, which runs both the death register and the National Registration (NRIC) register.
steps.summary: ICA keeps the national register of all persons in Singapore; the link from death registration to that register is administrative (both are ICA) and was not found in statute.

steps.title: CPF Board learns of the death
steps.summary: CPF Board guidance (not reachable here) states it is notified of deaths by ICA; the Act itself only lets the Board keep acting as if the member were alive until notified.

steps.title: CPF pays nominees or the Public Trustee
steps.who: The CPF Board; the Public Trustee where there is no nomination.
steps.summary: CPF savings pass outside the estate: to nominees, or, without a nomination, to the Public Trustee for distribution under the Intestate Succession Act or Muslim law.

registrationDeadlineDays.note: No family deadline to register; family report the death to a doctor 'as soon as practicable', and the doctor must submit particulars within 24 hours of examining the body.

informantDuty.note: Hospitals, relatives or occupiers must report to a doctor, but the duty to provide particulars for registration rests on the doctor (or Coroner).

medicalExaminerScrutiny.note: No independent review of doctor-certified deaths; reportable deaths go to the police and Coroner.

electronicRegistration.note: Doctors submit particulars to the Registrar-General through the electronic service it requires; the family does not attend a registry.

governmentPropagation.note: ICA, which registers deaths and holds the NRIC register, is understood to notify CPF and other agencies; not confirmed from statute or reachable agency pages.

certificateAccess.note: Registers closed to the public; extracts to close relatives, personal representatives and licensed insurers, others with a legitimate interest.

privateSectorVerification.note: Licensed insurers may obtain death-record extracts directly; no route for banks found.

gaps: www.ica.gov.sg, www.cpf.gov.sg and www.lifesg.gov.sg were refused by the egress proxy; ICA's death-registration and digital certificate pages and CPF's notification guidance are cited unverified.
No statutory provision found for automatic notification of deaths from ICA to CPF, IRAS, MOH/MediShield, the electoral roll (ELD) or LTA; the NRIC and CPF steps are unverified.
Whether the digital death certificate serves as the burial/cremation permit (Environmental Public Health (Cemeteries/Crematoria) rules) was not checked.
The Coroners Act Second Schedule (list of reportable deaths) was not read in full.
Probate and Administration Act / Public Trustee procedures and any bank-side verification route were not researched; no official death-data service for banks was found.
